shortlist.raw_text: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.

shortlist.summary: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. shortlist.raw_text: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

shortlist.raw_text: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

shortlist.raw_text: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

Article text (excerpt):
Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.
Nvidia’s CEO is reportedly the target of a ‘Chinese spy plot’ for intelligence on American AI chips.
China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times . The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.
Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.
The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang , was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

Coverage from Skoar! on MSN: "China allegedly hired AI executive to monitor Jensen Huang"
A businesswoman named Alice Huang was reportedly enlisted by China's intelligence agency to gather information on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Coverage from CNBC: "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI"
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker "absolutely must" work with Chinese AI companies on monitoring risks around the "potentially dangerous" technology.
"We absolutely should work with each other so that we advance the technology safely," he told CNBC during a media briefing on Wednesday evening in London.
Discussions around AI safety have intensified in recent months, after researchers from AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic called for a slowdown in developing the tech and warned of existential risks to humanity.
While OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have called for greater regulation , Huang has emerged as a prominent voice in opposition to that view.
Huang said that "dialogue" was the way to work with Chinese AI companies, adding that he has "dialogues with many of the researchers in China."
"We ought to enhance the dialogue," he added. "The United States should do it... I advocated that the U.K. do the same thing."
AI safety has become a key topic between the U.S. and Chinese governments, with both countries weighing how to address the risks posed by the rapidly advancing tech.
Prior to U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, in September, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level."
A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. "may have competition, but they may cooperate even more " in AI. "The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI," Xi said, per the readout.
Huang said that the U.K. is in a position "in the world to be able to be a convener of many of these dialogues" related to AI, because of the country's "intellectual capital."

Coverage from NDTV: "US Believes Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Had Romantic Relationship With Chinese 'Spy': Report"
Alice Huang was working for Beijing's Ministry of State Security, which was maneuvering to glean more detail about American artificial intelligence chips, according to the media reports ...

Background (Regulation of artificial intelligence in the United States, Wikipedia):
The United States federal government and state governments have developed some regulation of artificial intelligence, including executive orders, federal laws, and state laws. Federal agencies have also developed some sector-specific regulations related to AI.

Background (Ministry of State Security (China), Wikipedia):
The Ministry of State Security (MSS) is the principal civilian intelligence and security service of the People's Republic of China, responsible for foreign intelligence, counterintelligence, covert action, and the political security of the Chinese Communist Party. One of the largest and most secretive intelligence agencies in the world, it maintains powerful semi-autonomous branches in every province and city and administers the country's secret police, the State Security Police. The ministry is headquartered at Yidongyuan, a large compound in Beijing's Haidian district.

text:
China recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The goal was gathering intelligence on American AI chips and pushing for advanced chip access.

The price of controlling the hardware is now corporate espionage.

According to reporting from The New York Times, the Ministry of State Security enlisted Alice Huang because of her close relationship with the Nvidia chief.

She also maintains connections with executives at Gigabyte and other top levels of the industry.

President Trump was briefed on the relationship last year and took no action.

Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed door briefing on his interactions with her.

My read: the physical bottlenecks in AI are so severe that intelligence agencies are bypassing corporate lobbying entirely.

The facts come from reporting by The New York Times, CNBC, and Skoar! on MSN.

How far will governments go to secure advanced hardware?

Source: The Verge, with reporting from Skoar! on MSN and CNBC

Corporate lobbying is no longer the primary tool for gaining access to scarce AI hardware.
